d: Profile-driven VID/PID, product strings, HID descriptors, axis and button layout, and bus type. A Bluetooth controller carries the hardware and compatible IDs a real device of its transport carries, classic BTHENUM or LE BTHLEDevice, so it reports as Bluetooth, not as a USB device wearing its name. SDL3's controller database matches it, Steam recognizes it, Chrome identifies it, joy.cpl shows the right name.

Embedded profiles across 73 vendors: Xbox 360, Xbox Series, DualSense, Thrustmaster, Logitech, flight sticks, racing wheels, keyboards, mice, and more. Every device is a JSON file. Adding support for a new one means writing JSON, not modifying code.

Add a controller by writing a data-only JSON profile or by capturing one you already own, with no recompile. The SDK and the drivers hold no per-device code: battery scenario S88 fails on a device name, a vendor or product ID compared or switched on, or a profile field only one device sets, and the Sony feature answers, the Switch Pro's and Switch 2 Pro's protocols, the DualShock 3's sixaxis form and the XUSB companion's answers are all profile data. A report field's wire form is parameters: min and max, invert, a center for offset binary, a scale for motion counts, a battery level table, bit groups packed across frames, and a sensor clock that counts elapsed time. Profiles load strictly: a mistake refuses the file, and HMContext.ProfileLoadIssues lists it with the JSON path and the reason. A profile built in code meets the same checks at create, which throws HMProfileException before it touches the machine. A profile takes the feature answers, protocol and presentation it does not carry from a model it names with deviceModelFrom, or from identity defaults that keep a profile made outside the catalog behaving as its VID and PID did in 1.x. A device that builds its reports from its own state, as the Switch Pro, the Switch 2 Pro and the DualShock 3 do, carries a state block and report programs, compiled at build for the catalog and interpreted for your own profiles. HIDMaestroProfileCheck, in the release ZIP, checks a profile file as the SDK loads it and prints each problem with its JSON path. Adding a controller to a code-per-device emulator means writing and compiling a new device implementation. That difference is the whole point of the profile system. A device that carries several controllers in one report, and the commands it answers, are data too: the Wii U GameCube adapter's four ports and its command protocol are its profile, run by mechanisms any profile can use.

Point HMDeviceExtractor at any controller you have plugged in and get a ready-to-deploy profile back. Clone a DualSense and ship a 16-button variant that Windows, Steam, and games still see as a DualSense. Build a flight stick, racing wheel, or arcade panel from scratch with arbitrary VID/PID, axis count, button count, and resolution.

A profile can be a keyboard or a mouse. The catalog holds 51 keyboards and 52 mice from 32 vendors, each the report descriptor of a real device's keyboard or mouse interface. Raw Input lists each one as its kind, a Scroll Lock pressed on a virtual keyboard turns Scroll Lock on, and the mouse moves the cursor. SubmitKeyboard, SubmitMouse and SubmitConsumer pack into whatever reports the profile declares. Every report arrives: the driver confirms each one Windows takes, and a burst of 600 one-count moves lost nothing. If the consumer dies with a key held, the driver lets go of it, and the next session's cleanup removes the devices it left.

Two or more programs that embed HIDMaestro run on one machine, and none removes or writes to another's controllers, driver or files unless it calls the remove-everything cleanup. Each program claims ownership before its first machine-wide write, and each controller claims a transport index and an identity, all as named pipes that Windows deletes when the program ends. Asking for an identity another live program holds throws HMResourceInUseException. Sweeps remove only what exited programs left. Driver deploys take one machine-wide lock, never downgrade, and install the 2.0.0 driver over any older one, whatever runs on it. Device registrations and removals take another, so no program on this release registers a device while another removes one. While a program built on v1.12.0 runs, controllers take transport indices from 64, out of its way. That older program still removes every HIDMaestro device at its InstallDriver and first create, so programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0. Everything the SDK runs elevated is staged where only Administrators and SYSTEM can write, and checked against its SHA-256 first.

gamecube-adapter is Nintendo's WUP-028, the four-port adapter Melee players use, on the USB/IP transport. Its descriptors match 57 public dumps of the real adapter. Dolphin's and Slippi's own adapter code, compiled unmodified, reads all four ports, and so does SDL 3.4.18 built with libusb. The official SDL3 build for Windows has no libusb and lists no adapter, real or virtual. BindWinUsb() binds WinUSB to this one virtual adapter, so libusb hosts open it with no Zadig step. A restore never changes the driver of a devnode that is present. A real adapter that takes the instance after the virtual one is gone opens on WinUSB too, and after a kill it can open on WinUSB again at its next plug-in until a teardown, cleanup, reclaim, re-bind or follow-up finds the devnode gone and marks it to install Windows' HID driver. Each port has its own connection, input and rumble, and a controller connected to an empty port reports itself at rest. The adapter is a profile and no code: its ports, command protocol and WinUSB binding are JSON run by mechanisms any profile can use. A host poll interval can be set faster than the descriptor's 8 ms, as Melee players overclock the adapter.

HIDMaestro.Core.dll loads its catalog and runs in NativeAOT apps and in trimmed, self-contained, single-file apps, for x64 and ARM64. Profiles load through source-generated JSON and every Win32 call goes through LibraryImport. A Release build fails on any warning from the trim, single-file and AOT analyzers. At v1.12.0 both kinds of app loaded none of the 336 profiles.

Three composite personas present the whole USB device a real Valve controller presents: the Steam Deck's controller (five interfaces, reproduced from a real unit's lsusb dump), the wired 2015 Steam Controller (every descriptor verbatim from a real unit), and the 2026 Steam Controller. Steam files them under its own hardware rather than Generic DirectInput, answers arrive for the GET_REPORT interrogation Steam performs before claiming a device, and each packs its own wire format cross-checked against SDL's decoders.

t: A Switch Pro that answers back
d: The Switch Pro Controller is not a passive device: hosts drive a Nintendo subcommand handshake and stall without a device that answers. HIDMaestro answers it from the profile's data over the real Bluetooth wire, with a descriptor extracted byte-exact from a live Pro's SDP cache: SPI calibration reads, input-mode switch, and full-mode reports with gyro and accel every 15 ms on the device's own clock. switch-pro-usb is the same pad on its USB descriptor. SDL3 and Steam Input bind it as a real Bluetooth Pro Controller with motion and rumble.

switch2-pro-controller-composite presents a Switch 2 Pro Controller the way the pad appears over USB: HID on one interface and a vendor bulk pair on the other, with a real pad's descriptors byte for byte. Windows binds WinUSB to the second interface from the persona's own descriptors, with no driver install. Steam and SDL start it with the pad's own commands and then read its gyro and accelerometer, which the consumer submits in g and degrees per second. SDL reads 1 g and 100 degrees per second back within 1 percent on every axis. Rumble comes back decoded. DirectInput, WGI and browsers see a gamepad that never reports, as with a real pad, and switch2-pro-controller stays the profile for them.

dualshock-3-full presents a DualShock 3 the way Sony's sixaxis.sys driver and DsHidMini's SXS mode do on Windows, the form PCSX2 and RPCS3 read button pressure from. Cross, circle, square, triangle, L1, R1 and each d-pad direction take a pressure from 0 to 255, and L2 and R2 take theirs from the triggers. Motion, battery, rumble and the player LEDs come through as well. Stock SDL3 configured the way PCSX2 configures it reads every pressure axis. PCSX2 and RPCS3 themselves have not been run against it.

A real USB DualSense is a four-interface composite, and three profiles present all four. Windows gets the pad's own Speakers and Headset Microphone endpoints, and the 4-channel stream behind them carries the speaker on channels 1 and 2 and the voice-coil actuators on 3 and 4. That stream is the only path on Windows by which a game hands a controller its authored haptic waveforms. It reaches your code as UsbAudio.Output with each channel's role named. Nothing extra to install: the USB transport ships inside the DLL and deploys itself the first time you create one.

An embedded OpenVR driver presents a left and a right hand to SteamVR. The hands hold real SteamVR hand roles, serve the modern input system through a full input profile, and serve legacy GetControllerState readers through a shipped legacy binding. Controllers exist only while a consumer is live, so an idle machine shows no phantom devices. SteamVR is the one dependency, and it installs Steam-client-free and account-free via Valve's own steamcmd.
The input number is real propagation, measured over 10,000 single-press iterations and reproducible with one command. The methodology is published in the repository at docs/testing/latency.md.

A DualShock 4 create takes about half the time it took on 1.12.0, because a create installs the driver the store's search chose before instead of searching again. A game reads a DualShock 4 or DualSense report about 30 percent sooner after the submit. The driver and the XInput companion are built with the WDK's release optimization, and no submit, output report or USB/IP transfer allocates memory. The release notes give each path's numbers against 1.12.0.

Rumble, force feedback, and LED packets are signaled to the consumer per captured packet at ~0.18 ms median, roughly 50x faster than the 9.4 ms poll-quantized path it replaced. A controller at rest costs no measurable CPU unless its profile repeats its last report at rest as the real device does, as 21 profiles do: a DualSense over Bluetooth every 1.25 ms, a DualShock 4 every 4 ms.

Standard profiles use shared memory between the SDK and UMDF2 drivers. Input and output are signaled per frame or packet. Composite profiles use the bundled USB/IP transport over a loopback connection.

VIIPER's published Windows figure, 168 µs, is localhost-only. Running it over an actual network, the thing the project is named for, adds roughly 1 to 5 ms on wired LAN or 10 to 50 ms over Wi-Fi on top of that figure, a caveat its docs mention only in passing. It also batches reports every millisecond, capping the update rate at 1000 Hz. HIDMaestro's input is event-driven with no fixed cap.

Standard profiles keep controller traffic in shared memory. Composite profiles use a local loopback USB/IP connection. Applications can build network sharing above the SDK, as PadForge does with Remote Link.

t: Fast to start, fast to recover
d: When the installed driver already matches, InstallDriver() completes in ~40-60 ms and a consumer goes from process start to a live controller in about a second. If the consuming app is force-closed mid-session, the next launch evicts the orphaned devices and has the first controller live again in ~2.3 s, measured with an Xbox Series BT profile in the mix, the deepest teardown stack.

DirectInput sees correct axes and buttons. XInput sees separate triggers in one slot. SDL3/HIDAPI sees the right identity and bus type. The browser sees a STANDARD GAMEPAD with separate triggers. WGI sees one Gamepad. RawInput sees the same device as all of them, at the same time.

No hard limit on simultaneous virtual controllers. Tested with 6 mixed types, correct per-controller ordering across every API. XInput caps Xbox-family profiles at its own 4 slots. Non-Xbox profiles run beyond it. Controllers from several programs that embed HIDMaestro coexist on one machine, each program keeping its own.
Create and remove controllers on the fly, about 200 ms for a single controller as measured before v2.0.0. Live-swap a controller's profile mid-session. No reboots, no leftover devices.

HID PID 1.0 answers for DirectInput force-feedback games, plus rumble and haptic output events the consumer routes to real hardware. The driver accepts the writes and raises them to your application in real time.

Standard profiles run through the Windows UMDF2 stack and a locally trusted signing certificate. Composite profiles use the bundled Microsoft-signed USB/IP transport. The installation does not enable Windows test-signing mode.

InstallDriver() creates a locally trusted certificate, signs the driver, and installs it. No EV certificate, no test-signing mode, no reboot. When the installed driver already matches, the call completes in ~40-60 ms. Only one program deploys at a time. An older driver is upgraded whatever runs on it, and a newer one is never downgraded.

HIDMaestro.Core.dll contains the 337-profile catalog, a driver and helper payload for x64 and one for ARM64, the signing tools, and the signed USB/IP installers for both. It picks the set matching the machine. The OpenVR plugin is x64 for its SteamVR host. A source build can leave out the ARM64 payload or the USB/IP transport, and HMBuildInfo reports what a build carries.

The battery has 99 scenarios covering lifecycle, encoders, consumer APIs, USB/IP, VR, the battery reply a pad gives XInput, device identity across nine lives per family, the driver catalogs for both architectures, the DualShock 3 and 4 reports against the programs that read them, the Switch 2 Pro persona against a capture of a real pad, the registry keys a virtual shares with real devices, every catalog keyboard and mouse through Raw Input, programs running side by side as separate processes, NativeAOT and single-file apps, the GameCube adapter persona through Dolphin, Slippi and SDL, every raw value of every catalog conversion through the SDK's rounding, the Sony, Valve and Nintendo vendor-blob reports against golden bytes, profiles and device models loaded strictly, every report program three ways, the protocol engine and device clock, the version contract on the live driver, a Joy-Con built from the Switch Pro's mechanisms, and the SDK and drivers checked for device shortcuts. Production signing and the full HIDMaestro integration gate remain pending.

The battery checks more than HIDMaestro's own decode of its own encode. A stock upstream SDL3 build reads the Valve personas and must bind each with its own Valve driver, and a scenario starts the actual Steam client and asserts it claims and classifies them. Another runs Steam's own firmware updater, which must see the 2026 Steam Controller persona and offer it no update. Stock SDL3 arms the Bluetooth DualShock 4 persona itself and must keep reading it, and opens the DualShock 3 persona the way PCSX2 configures it. SDL3 with libusb starts the Switch 2 Pro persona and reads its motion back on every axis, and the Steam client must add it and keep reading it. The decoders Steam Input is built on are the judges. Dolphin's and Slippi's own adapter code, compiled unmodified, reads the GameCube adapter persona, and SDL built with libusb lists one gamepad per port.

Composite Sony, Valve and Nintendo profiles use the bundled usbip-win2 0.9.8.1 kernel transport, redistributed unmodified and checked against its pinned SHA-256 at build and again before execution. The SDK installs it silently on a machine that has none, with the smallest set of components its installer allows, and never invokes the vendor uninstaller. A machine HIDMaestro put on 0.9.7.7 or 0.9.7.5 is moved to 0.9.8.1 automatically, through one Windows driver update that leaves the root-hub filter alone, in a session where the controller is still unused.
Free and open source. Use it in your own projects, commercial or otherwise, with no restrictions.

The HID driver, the XInput companion and the device helper are built for ARM64 as well as x64, and the INFs carry an NTARM64 section. HIDMaestro.Core.dll holds both sets and installs the one matching the operating system. Composite personas use a Microsoft-signed ARM64 build of the USB transport. The release has an ARM64 ZIP with an ARM64 test app and profile extractor. Use v1.9.1 or later on ARM64. The battery builds the ARM64 driver catalog on every run, and no ARM64 machine has run the battery yet.
Windows 10/11 on x64 and Windows 11 on ARM64, with .NET 10 and a 64-bit consumer. Every release has a ZIP for each architecture.
If you want to use HIDMaestro through a UI instead of code, install PadForge. It wraps this SDK with a full input-mapping app.
